idiom_name: @JvmInline value class (single-property wrapper erased to its underlying type)
implementation_notes: Kotlin's answer to the allocation a wrapper class adds is the inline value class, introduced with exactly this problem: the docs note that wrapping a value 'introduces runtime overhead due to additional heap allocations' and that 'instances of the inline class will be represented using this single property', so an id, password or meter type can carry domain meaning without allocating - the compiler prefers the underlying representation and only boxes where it must. That replaces the classic hand-written buffer for fixed-shape wrappers only: a value class has exactly one property, no backing fields, no lateinit/delegated properties, and the JVM still cannot embed a variable-size buffer inside an object, so short strings and small vectors keep using primitive arrays, ByteBuffer/off-heap storage or a reused buffer. Prefer the value class for wrappers and the array/pool for variable-size payloads; a hand-rolled inline buffer has no JVM representation to build on.
code_sketch:
@JvmInline
value class UserId(val raw: Long)        // no wrapper allocation at use sites

data class Row(val id: UserId, val len: Int)

fun lookup(id: UserId): Row = table[id.raw]   // compiled as lookup-<hash>(long)

fun asAny(x: UserId): Any = x            // boxed here: used as another type
pitfalls: Boxing is silent and situational: a value class is boxed when used as a generic type argument, as an interface implementation, as a nullable, or when stored in an array - so the allocation returns exactly where such types usually travel (collections, framework APIs, serialization).

The single-property restriction is hard: no backing fields, no secondary state, no lateinit or delegated properties, and referential equality is forbidden - a wrapper that needs a cache or a second field cannot be a value class and must stay a regular class.

Mangled JVM signatures (compute-<hash>(long)) surprise Java callers, reflection-based DI frameworks and nullability-checked interop; annotate with @JvmName or compile the class to a boxed form when Java code must see it.
sources: Kotlin documentation, Inline value classes - 'it introduces runtime overhead due to additional heap allocations ... instances of the inline class will be represented using this single property', with the representation and boxing rules: https://kotlinlang.org/docs/inline-classes.html
